Metropolis. Fritz Lang's 1927 German science-fiction epic. The film depicts a futuristic city divided between a wealthy elite living in gleaming towers and enslaved workers toiling underground. A visionary masterpiece of production design and thematic ambition, it pioneered cinematic science fiction and German Expressionist technique while exploring capitalism, class struggle, and technological dehumanization.

Lang's original cut ran about two and a half hours, though it was heavily edited and lost in various markets. The plot centers on a love between Freder, son of the city's master, and Maria, a worker. Their connection ignites a revolution and challenge to the ruling class. The robot Maria—a mechanical woman created to control the working class—became an icon of cinema. Her dance scene remains unforgettable.

The film employs German Expressionist visual language: stark shadows, distorted angles, and monumental architecture convey the city's oppressive structure. Special effects were groundbreaking for the time: the robot transformation, miniatures for city shots, matte paintings, and the metropolis set itself, which took over a year to construct. The city's design was handled by Erich Kettelhut, making this Germany's most expensive film ever made at that time.

Reconstructions in 2008 and 2010 restored much lost footage, though the full original remains partially lost. Metropolis influenced virtually every subsequent science-fiction film and visual tradition, from Blade Runner to anime aesthetics, establishing the visual and thematic language of the genre for the twentieth century and beyond.
